questions.stem: The International Space Station orbits Earth at about 400 km altitude. Astronauts inside appear to float. Why do they experience 'weightlessness'?

options.text: There is no gravity at that altitude
They are too far from Earth for gravity to have any effect
The ISS and astronauts are in continuous free fall together -- they are falling towards Earth at the same rate as the station moves forward
The ISS generates an anti-gravity field inside the station

questions.explanation: At 400 km altitude, gravity is still about 90% as strong as at Earth's surface. The astronauts appear weightless because the ISS and everything inside it are in continuous free fall. The station moves forward fast enough that as it falls, it continually misses Earth's surface -- this IS an orbit. Since everything falls at the same rate, there is no relative motion between the astronauts and the station floor, creating the sensation of weightlessness.

questions.stem: A geostationary satellite orbits Earth with a period of exactly 24 hours. Why is this orbital period useful for communications satellites?

options.text: It means the satellite can cover every point on Earth's surface
It means the satellite stays above the same point on Earth's surface, so ground-based dish antennas do not need to track it
It means the satellite is the closest possible to Earth
It means the satellite travels the fastest of any orbit

questions.explanation: A geostationary satellite orbits with the same period as Earth's rotation (24 hours) above the equator, so it stays above the same point on the surface. This means satellite dishes on the ground can be fixed in position -- they do not need to track a moving satellite. Geostationary orbits are at about 36,000 km altitude, not close to Earth (C). They are actually slower than low-orbit satellites (D). They can only 'see' part of Earth's surface (A), which is why multiple geostationary satellites are needed for global coverage.

questions.stem: Two satellites orbit Earth: Satellite A at 500 km altitude and Satellite B at 20,000 km altitude. Which satellite has the longer orbital period?

options.text: Satellite A, because it is closer to Earth and moves faster
Satellite B, because a higher orbit has a longer circumference and the satellite moves more slowly
Both have the same orbital period
It depends on the mass of the satellite

questions.explanation: Higher orbits have longer orbital periods for two reasons: the circumference is greater (more distance to travel) and the satellite moves more slowly (weaker gravitational pull means less centripetal acceleration). This is Kepler's third law. Satellite A orbits faster and has a shorter period. The orbital period does not depend on the mass of the satellite (D) -- only on the orbital radius and the mass of the body being orbited.

questions.stem: A polar orbit satellite passes over both the North and South poles as Earth rotates beneath it. This type of orbit is used for:

options.text: Television broadcasting to fixed dish antennas
Earth observation and weather monitoring, because it can eventually scan the entire surface
GPS navigation only
Keeping the satellite stationary above one point

questions.explanation: Polar orbit satellites pass over both poles while Earth rotates beneath them. Over successive orbits, different strips of the surface pass below the satellite, eventually allowing it to image the entire Earth. This makes polar orbits ideal for Earth observation, weather monitoring, and mapping. TV broadcasting (A) typically uses geostationary satellites. GPS (C) uses medium Earth orbits. A polar orbit satellite is not stationary above one point (D) -- that describes a geostationary satellite.

questions.stem: What provides the centripetal force that keeps a satellite in orbit around Earth?

options.text: The satellite's engines, which must fire continuously
The gravitational attraction between the satellite and Earth
The magnetic field of the Earth
The push from solar radiation

questions.explanation: Gravity provides the centripetal force needed to keep a satellite on its curved orbital path. Once in orbit, no engine thrust is needed (A) -- the satellite falls freely under gravity. In the vacuum of space, there is virtually no friction to slow it down. Earth's magnetic field (C) does not keep satellites in orbit. Solar radiation pressure (D) is extremely small and is not what maintains an orbit.
